hits.name: Shruti
hits.hook: Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.
hits.original_en:
Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.

109 million parameters beat 72 billion.

He has spent years saying scale is not the thing that makes a model understand the world. Meta bet the other way. He left in November and started his own lab in Paris.

Last Thursday he published the proof.

The theory everyone has been running on since 2024 is that if you train models big enough, on text, on images, on sound, they all end up with the same picture of reality inside them. Size does it. Nobody ever proved that part.

Randall Balestriero and LeCun proved it. And the proof says size was never doing the work.

What does the work is which two things you show a model together.

A photo and the caption of that photo are two views of one thing. Models trained on pairs like that get there fast.

Two paragraphs pulled from the same document are not two views of one thing. Models trained on those get there slowly and expensively.

Next word prediction is the second kind. That is what every chatbot in the world runs on.

In their tests the first method reached the same understanding after 21.6 million examples. Next word prediction needed 900 million.

And a 109 million parameter text model ended up closer to an image model's view of the world than a 72 billion parameter language model was.

660 times smaller.
hits.draft_en:
109 million parameters vs 72 billion, and the tiny one won

a text model 660 times smaller landed nearer to an image model's internal picture of reality than the giant language model did

Yann LeCun and Randall Balestriero shipped the proof last Thursday. it breaks the core assumption the field has leaned on since 2024: feed a big enough model text, pictures and audio and they all converge on one shared world view, purely from size. nobody ever proved that bit

per their paper, size isn't the lever. pairing is: what two inputs sit next to each other in training

- an image and its caption describe a single thing from two angles, so learning is quick

- two passages lifted from one document don't, so learning is slow and expensive

chatbots run on next word prediction, which sits in that slow bucket

the numbers from their tests: 21.6 million examples for the paired setup to reach the same understanding, 900 million for next word prediction

LeCun has argued for years that scaling alone doesn't create understanding. Meta took the opposite bet, he walked out in November, and now runs a lab of his own in Paris
hits.video_tip: talking-head with two big on-screen numbers (109 million vs 72 billion), then a simple two-column graphic: photo + caption pair vs two paragraphs, ending on 21.6 million vs 900 million

hits.name: Peter Yang
hits.hook: I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.
hits.original_en:
I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.

Some takes I loved:

1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.”

Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat.

2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?”

Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place.

3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?”

Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first.

4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.”

Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.”

5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.”

Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first.

6. “Let your kid be your creative director.”

Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode. It’s live on Spotify.

📌 Watch now: https://t.co/8hLt6x6atQ

Thanks to our sponsors:

@WisprFlow: 4x faster than typing with your voice https://t.co/oqHJ8bN3ll

@RiversidedotFM: All-in-one AI studio for podcasts and video https://t.co/uWnS6aiMPE
hits.draft_en:
6 product rules from Jaclyn (@jacalulu), PM Director at Google Labs, on how Gemini 4 changed the way Google builds

- a doc should never take longer to read than it took to write. AI can help you think, but you stay in the driver's seat

- the question moved from "can we build it" to "should this exist at all". if a couple of agents could knock it out over a weekend, it's probably not durable

- ask if your product needs a person or a UI in the first place. chores get built for agents first, while humans keep coming back to make things, to learn or for fun

- don't hand users exactly what they ask for. keep talking to them, dig to the root problem and fix it in a way they'd never have pictured

- stop expecting people to write elaborate prompts. her team built Pomelli, Google's tool that helps SMBs make on-brand content, and it reads your website to learn the business before anything else

- let your kid run creative. her 5-year-old chooses the voices, names every character and gives notes on each cut of their podcast Maya and the Fog, while the agent produces it. it's on Spotify now

full conversation: https://t.co/8hLt6x6atQ

hits.name: Trace Cohen
hits.hook: A startup growing 100% a year can actually become less attractive to acquire.
hits.original_en:
A startup growing 100% a year can actually become less attractive to acquire.

Imagine a company doing $20M in revenue, growing 100% annually, with an acquisition offer of $200M.

Pretty incredible outcome.

But management decides to raise another round at a $500M valuation instead.

Two years later, revenue hits $80M, but growth slows to 30%. Buyers now offer 4x revenue, or $320M.

The company quadrupled its revenue, doubled down on its ambitions, and ended up with a potential exit worth less than its last funding valuation.

All hypothetical, but the math is very real.

Sometimes the hardest part of building a billion-dollar company is knowing when you’ve already built a great one.

The vast majority of recurring ghostwriting services fall in the $3,000 to $7,000 per month range.

Stop billing hourly. Package your asset, set the outcome, and anchor between $3k and $7k.

→ It publishes your website on the internet.
→ Free Vercel account for personal websites.

→ Pick a new, empty folder on your desktop.

"/goal Remake [THE WEBSITE URL YOU CHOSE] with github .com/rubenhassid1/remake until its report says REMAKE COMPLETE, or stop after 100 turns."

hits.hook: Give me 3 mins, and I will make you better at Claude than 90% of people.
hits.original_en:
Give me 3 mins, and I will make you better at Claude than 90% of people.

First up, delete these things from your claude:

1. Go to Claude → Account → “Instructions for Claude." Empty the box.
2. Claude left bar → Customize → Skills. Remove anything you uploaded about yourself.
3. Skills → Yours → Search “writing” → Turn off.
4. Claude Setting → Memory → Turn it off.
5. Any over-organised folder you maintain.
6. Subfolders inside the folder in folder (of course).
7. about-me .md you wrote in the past.
8. Anti-AI writing file (download the skill instead)
9. All the folder protocol in Claude instructions.
10. Forget the habit of choosing Chat-Cowork-Code
11. Any prompt library. You just need one.
12. 100 Projects with 100+ files, rules & constraints.
13. Any Claude skill written for old models.
14. Skills that overlap with other skills.
15. Delete global instructions. It ignores it anyway.
16. Habit of using "High" for grammar tasks.
17. Habit of switching on connectors when you don't need them, because "just in case."
18. Claude Plugin pack for one-off tasks.
19. Someone else's copy-pasted prompts.

Now keep or set up only these 6 things:

1. You only need this one prompt to start a chat

"Goal: [what you want, and what it's for] Context: [who it's for, what you already have, what good looks like] Before you start, restate in your own words what you think my goals are and the problem I'm trying to solve. If you need more context, ask me questions."

2. Ask for HTML (trust me).

Stop asking for a Word file, a PowerPoint or a PDF.

Try asking for HTML. Add this line to your prompt:

"Make it an HTML page."

3. Switch your massive folder to short memory

Open the Claude desktop app & select your old folder (mine was called CLAUDE COWORK) and copy a long prompt from this guide to turn into a short memory Claude can keep: https://t.co/NYWCbdGAVl

The prompt will start the process, then answer every question. You'll get the block to copy. Go to Memory → at the bottom, paste it → it will update your memory.

FYI: Delete this entire setup (again) in the coming 6 months. By then, we might have Claude-7 with the kind of speed Anthropic is releasing new models.

PS: I would rather read the free guide instead of this post: https://t.co/NYWCbdGAVl

hits.hook: the highest alpha play right now is so simple most people will never do it...
hits.original_en:
the highest alpha play right now is so simple most people will never do it...

make a harness that works for YOU

it'll 10x the quality and speed of your AI outputs.

paste this ONE prompt into your agent:

---------start of the prompt----------------

Build me a Langfuse-style observability dashboard from my own AI coding sessions for the last 7 days.

SOURCES (read locally, read-only):
- Claude Code: ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl
- Codex: ~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl (and ~/.codex/history.jsonl)
Never print secrets, keys or full prompt text. Snippets max 10 words, with keys, paths, URLs and long ids stripped.

STEP 1. Write a stdlib-only Python script that computes, per tool:
- sessions per day, user prompts, tool calls by tool name, failed tool calls by tool and error type
- models used, tokens (input, output, cache read/write) per model per day
- tool-call latency p50/p95, overall and per tool; session length p50/p95
- top sessions by tokens, longest sessions, retries (same tool call repeated after an error)
- prompts clustered into task types (build, debug, deploy, research, writing, UI, review, other)
- sessions grouped by project (working directory), with subagent runs flagged
If a log doesn't record something, write "not logged". Never invent numbers.
Save the result as harness-summary.json.

STEP 2. Render a single-file dashboard.html (dark, animated numbers and charts):
- Summary strip: total tool calls, prompts, error rate, tokens, p95 latency
- Traces table: one row per session (tool, project, start, duration, prompts, tool calls, errors, tokens, model); search, filter by tool, sort, toggle to hide subagent runs
- Trace detail: click a session to see a waterfall of its turns and tool calls with ok/error and duration
- Sessions by project, tokens over time by model, a model table (tokens, error rate)
- Latency view per tool, and an error explorer grouped by tool and error type
- Heuristic scores (tool success rate, retries, per-session health), clearly labeled "heuristic"
Cap embedded traces at the top 200 sessions by tokens if the file gets too big.

STEP 3. From the data, write HARNESS.md proposing changes to CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md:
- Model routing: which model for which task type, based on what I used and what failed
- Tools: keep (high use, low failure), fix (high failure), cut (rarely used)
- Skills: one for every task type I repeated 3+ times, with a trigger line and steps
- Guardrails: my top 3 failure patterns and a check that prevents each
- Budget: my top 5 token sinks and one change that would cut each
Cite the sessions behind each suggestion.

STEP 4. Show me the 5 headline numbers and the proposed diff before changing any config. I'll review weekly and change only what the data shows.

--------end of the prompt-------------

hits.hook: i'm using grokbot to find my clients.
hits.original_en:
i'm using grokbot to find my clients.

if you've got 30 minutes this weekend, steal this setup and start building:

first, tell it what you sell, who it's for and give it a few examples of messages you'd actually send.

then build these 3 agents:

1. lead list builder
researches each person and saves why they might be a fit, where it found them and how i could reach out.

i want actual research behind the message. give me something about this person i can start a conversation with.

2. pipeline tracker
keeps track of who i've contacted, what happened and when i should follow up.

i tell it when i've sent something or gotten a reply. if i don't log it, it doesn't know. you still have to do your part here.

3. outreach drafter
takes that research and writes a short message i'd actually send.

my rules are pretty simple:
- 25–50 words
- open with something specific about them
- ask one easy question
- don't ask for a call straight away
- don't make up customer stories
- offer my free personal brand starter kit only when it makes sense

for email, it gives me a subject line too. if replying to their post makes more sense, it drafts a useful reply. everyone doesn't need a dm pitch.

i read it, edit it and send it myself. then i log what happened so the next message has context.

that's a pretty useful way to spend part of your weekend.

excluded_hits.hook: My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.
excluded_hits.original_en:
My unfiltered thoughts on personal agents.

Grokbot has the best UI and it’s arguably the best overall. In a lot of ways they’re ahead. Their desktop app feels the best, and their multi-bot coordination is great: you can set a team lead and it passes tasks to the other bots. Grokbot also has the best “webhook” feature, which means you can easily turn outside events into triggers that start your agents. That speeds up background workflows like watching your email, Slack and more. It also has Cursor integration, so for bigger tasks Grokbot can spin up a Cursor cloud session with any model (until OpenAI cuts SpaceX off from their models, which I think will happen soon). Unfortunately, running frontier models through Cursor costs more than Claude or Codex. Still, they’re the only ones embracing a team of agents. It’s a really cool idea, but the more bots you have, the more time you spend managing and maintaining them. I’m starting to think one bot with different threads/channels is the right answer, which I’ll get to with Claude Duet.

dots by OpenAI is rough around the edges right now, but it’s probably the most powerful if you use Codex, which I do. dots can spin up Codex sessions in the cloud or locally on your computer. So if you have coding or video editing workflows that need your local files, this is very useful. Codex computer use is also the best in the world: your dot can spin up a local Codex session that fully controls your computer, as long as it’s on. Their real-time voice is incredible. If you have your email and work tools connected, try this: go on a walk with headphones in, ask the agent to summarize your emails, have it draft replies and read them back to you, then send them off. If I remember right, this is close to a workflow you (Tim) used to have with your VAs before AI. It’s my favorite use case for personal agents. The one downside is that you have to call your agent, and it’s an awful experience. It literally rings, and it’s annoying.

Muse by Meta is a toy. I’ve talked to a bunch of finance people I play poker with who all tried it and set up automations, and they all said it doesn’t reliably do what they want. It’s fast, and its user numbers will probably keep growing. But it’s basically free: you get a TON of usage without paying a dime. That’s NOT a trade I’m willing to make. An agent doing high-leverage tasks should be running at the Opus 5.5 or GPT 6.1 Sol level.

Claude Duet - is in early access, so unfortunately not everyone can use it yet. First things first, it runs on Opus 5.5, the best model in the world. I’ve only had access for 72 hours, but Duet feels different from the others. It’s not a personified agent like Grokbot, dot or Muse, which gives it a more professional vibe that I like. When you ask your Duet agent to do something, it spins up a task, which is a new chat thread. All your threads show up in a Tasks tab, so it’s easy to see everything Duet is working on or has finished. And instead of creating more agents (like Grokbot), you create channels, just like Slack (I can tell @anthropic is Slack-pilled). I have a content channel, a finances channel, etc., which keeps different kinds of tasks separate. The only other app I’ve seen do this is Buzz by @jack, and it’s a good experience. Their strong point is documents (artifacts). If you want decks, high-quality docs or design mockups, Opus just wins. Period. It’s not close right now. Their weak point is real-time voice. It’s the worst of the bunch and borderline unusable, though I think they only added it a few days ago.

Instinct lives in iMessage, has no app, and doesn’t do anything notable besides show you product suggestions you didn’t ask for. (Not ads, according to their team.)

My hot take: 
The VM is overrated. SpaceX, OpenAI and Meta all talk about the VM your agent can use and feature it in their marketing. It’s not as useful as you’d think, because more and more websites block bots that visit their site on the cloud VM. All of these companies promise their agents can make payments, but most payments either take forever or get blocked altogether. SpaceX has a cool workaround with Grokbot that routes traffic through your computer so it uses your IP address. But I’d much rather the agent just USE my computer for the task, like dot does by handing it off to Codex. Also, i don't think normal people care about the virtual computer. If anything they get offended they have to "stream a computer". 

The problem with personal agents: by the time you read this, pick one, and test it for 7 days, every one of them will have released 10 new features and the whole landscape will have changed. It’s nearly impossible to keep up.

Parasite SEO: 11 sneaky ways to get on page 1 of Google in 2-3 weeks👇

Parasite SEO means hacking Google by posting content, written in a special way, on websites Google and ChatGPT already trust, so they show and cite you

1/ Write about next year before anyone else
->  Nobody has written “best X 2027” yet. The first good page usually takes the top spot and keeps it

2/ Publish a “research paper” about your niche on arXiv or Zenodo
->  These are free research sites ChatGPT trusts. A paper like “The best office chairs for back pain” can become the source it quotes

3/ Launch a free Chrome extension
->  Every extension gets its own page in Google’s Chrome store with a link to your site, and that page can show up on Google

4/ Write short LinkedIn articles 
->  Under ~330 words with the answer at the top. LinkedIn articles are the #1 source for Gemini and Google AI Overview answers

5/ Publish job listings with your brand name and no link
->  Applicants search your brand name on Google to find you. The more people search for you, the more Google trusts you

6/ Buy an old website in your niche
->  It already shows up on Google. Point its pages to your site and you take over its spots

67/ Make a spreadsheet that shows up on Google
->  Make a “Best X tools 2026” table in Google Sheets with your brand first and click Publish to web. Now it’s a public page on Google’s own site

8/ Hide a keyword in your LinkedIn article’s web address
->  LinkedIn creates the web address from your first title and never changes it. Title it “YourBrand: the best AI SEO tool”, publish, then change the title. The address keeps the keyword

9/ Publish 10 Gamma presentations
->  Gamma is a free slides app, and every deck you publish becomes a web page Google can show. Make 1 deck per search, like “best CRM for dentists”, with a link to your site

10/ Publish a free page on GitHub
->  GitHub is a site developers trust, and Google shows its pages fast. Great for tools and tech products

11/ Answer popular Quora questions that have almost no answers
->  Search Google for site: quora “your topic” “1 answer”. Thousands of readers, only 1 other answer to beat

Prepared by growth hackers at Ryze AI, the AI agent for paid ads and SEO/GEO

hits.original_en:
nobody will tell you this... but your AI agent is probably slower and dumber because you gave it too many subagents

Anthropic's own team tested it: one agent with skills often beat the multi-agent setup on quality, cost and speed

- ~2x faster runs for one customer
- 80%+ smaller Claude Code system prompt on newer models
- tool choice breaks past 30-50 tools

paste this prompt to fold your subagents back in the way Anthropic recommends:
-----------------------------------------------------
audit my agent setup and fold my subagents back into one main agent. don't edit any files until i say ok.

1. MAP: list every subagent with its prompt, its tools and when it gets called. flag any that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or usually run together.
2. SKILLS: turn each subagent's instructions into a skill. give each one a one-line description of when to use it, and load the full steps only when they're needed.
3. TOOLS: turn the API calls into tools grouped by what the user is trying to do, not one tool per API. keep the total under 30.
4. TESTS: before changing anything, write 10 test tasks that cover every chain of agents and every rule the agent must never break.
5. FOLD: fold in one subagent at a time. run every test task twice. keep a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, it needs fresh context for parallel work, or the main agent's context gets bloated without it.

show me the full plan first and wait for my ok.
------------------------------------------------------
hits.draft_en:
how to get 2x faster AI agent runs and cut your Claude Code system prompt by 80%

spawning 10 subagents slows execution and bloats context - Anthropic tested folding them back into 1 main agent with on-demand skills:

- map the handoffs: list every subagent and flag any that chain outputs or read the same state
- convert to skills: turn each subagent prompt into a modular skill with a 1-line trigger so full instructions only load when called
- cap tool count: group raw API endpoints by user intent and keep total tools under 30 so tool selection stays sharp
- benchmark before cutting: write 10 test tasks and fold 1 subagent at a time, keeping only subagents that need isolated parallel context

i grew a company from 0 to $4M in a year. 

i've led marketing at 3 multimillion-dollar companies.

11 marketing principles i still use every week:

1) say one thing. buyers remember one sentence from you. pick it on purpose.

2) the buyer's words beat yours. steal phrases from sales calls, reviews and support tickets.

3) name what you replace. "better than nothing" is a weak pitch. "better than the spreadsheet you hate" sells.

4) sell the after. show what their week looks like once it works.

5) put proof next to the claim. a number under a promise does more than a row of logos.

6) specific beats clever. "set up in 4 minutes" beats any pun you'll ever write.

7) the founder is your best marketer. buyers trust a person before they trust a logo.

8) price is part of the message. a cheap price tells buyers it's a small problem.

9) write for the skeptic. once the doubter nods, everyone else follows.

10) repeat yourself. you'll get sick of your message long before the market hears it once.

11) taste is the edge now. AI made average copy free. buyers pay for judgment.

how to structure a 4-block prompt template so Grok Bot or Claude Code executes complex tasks on the 1st run

vague 1-line prompts force your agent to guess your file paths, tone, and acceptance criteria

wrap every high-stakes task in this 4-block template inside `task_prompt.md`

> `[context]` - point the Grok Bot or Claude Code agent to the exact 2 local files and schema it must read first

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.

hits.hook: Just spoke to the Head of AI at a huge company.
hits.original_en:
Just spoke to the Head of AI at a huge company. 

The #1 thing they're struggling with is... what do I do with the AI laggards at our company? 

Like most companies, they’ve found that a Super Pareto Principle is true within their org. 10% of their employees are responsible for 90% of the uplift in productivity/token usage from software engineering to non-technical knowledge work. 

They’ve spent a lot of time & resources on AI enablement from LLM foundations to function-specific trainings and skill building. And yet, the power law of productivity increases hasn’t budged. 

So now they’re left with a few sobering thoughts and hard questions:
1) 90% of people are overpaid and 10% are underpaid 
2) We’d be better off allocating tokens proportionally to the power law, but how do we do that without killing culture? 
3) Significant layoffs are likely warranted and wouldn’t impact overall output, but cultural backlash is a big concern? 
4) How do we hire more power law people as a non technology company? 
5) Is all of our efforts on training and enablement ACTUALLY worth it? 
6) How do we not experience a brain drain where the top 10% all leave because they want to be surrounded by other AI-native 10x’ers?

hits.name: Alex Lieberman
hits.hook: Experian, a $35 billion business with roots dating back to 1826, is surprisingly AI-native.
hits.original_en:
Experian, a $35 billion business with roots dating back to 1826, is surprisingly AI-native.

Its new Chief AI Officer, Vijay Mehta, broke down the credit bureau’s end-to-end AI strategy. 

Complete list of notes...

Big takeaways: 
• Experian is well past proof of concept, with AI capabilities running in production throughout the company. 
• The next stage is what Mehta calls "reimagination." Redesigning how work gets done through delegation to agents vs. prompting chat bots.  
• Adoption is close to universal. 85% of employees actively use the company's AI tools, 88% of developers use coding assistants, and employees built more than 6,000 custom GPTs by the first half of fiscal 2026. 
• They're seeing real ROI. It's measured in time savings, time to value, quality, velocity and traditional before and after financial metrics, not in adoption or token use.

How they built the foundation: 
• Within months of ChatGPT's launch, they trained thousands of employees and put AI policies and guardrails in place. 
• AI traffic was routed through a control plane that gives them observability, monitoring and security. 
• They wrote a GenAI risk framework and built the Experian GenAI Platform, an internal system that lets employees build internal-facing & and customer-facing apps, while accessing company data securely. 
• They rolled out a coding assistant to their large developer base and built their own Experian GPT into products like a digital financial assistant and their Ascend platform. 
• They created a GenAI Center of Expertise, which now sits under Mehta's AI office. 
• Since then, AI has spread across software development, analytics and business operations.

AI inside the employee experience: 
• MyCareer platform recommends learning and career moves and helps managers spot skills gaps. 
• Nadia, an internal AI coach, helps employees set goals, build development plans and prepare for performance reviews. 
• Nadia also gives leaders personalized coaching and 360-degree feedback.

On models and cost: 
• "Not everybody needs the most advanced frontier model. Most workloads can be done with a free or very low-cost model." 
• He compares reaching for a frontier model by default to using a sledgehammer on a job that needs a much smaller tool. 
• They run a mix of open-weight models adapted to their own environment and frontier models accessed through AWS Bedrock. 
• The control plane routes each workload to a model based on the task, language, region and regulatory requirements.

On agent safety: 
• Guardrails are designed into the architecture from the beginning instead of being added later. 
• Their Agent Operating System runs on that control plane, so it can sandbox, monitor and stop an agent process when necessary. "The ability to kill a process, the ability to kill a process, I will repeat that, we've got all of that built in." 
• Their risk profile differs from the frontier labs' because their systems work over a defined body of financial and identity data, without broad access to the internet. "We start with our corpus of data and we put controls around that. And we know exactly how the data is moving."

What the CAIO role actually is: 
• Experian is a big company split into many business units. His job is one common AI strategy and direction: "to make sure that we are all marching in the same direction." 
• He accelerates the AI agenda both internally and externally. 
• Risk, security, compliance and partner choices all come together in the AI office.

AI as the new middleman: 
• Consumers increasingly start their financial journey inside an AI assistant instead of going to Experian or a bank, so Experian is meeting them there. 
• It's the first personal finance app integrated with Google's Gemini. US consumers who connect their Experian accounts can ask Gemini about their FICO credit rating and what's affecting it. 
• Inside ChatGPT it has launched personal loan shopping, credit card shopping and an insurance marketplace. 
• On the enterprise side, ServiceNow is the first integration partner for its Agent Operating System. Under a multiyear partnership, ServiceNow agents tap Experian's Ascend data and decisioning from inside enterprise workflows. 
• It also launched Agent Trust, which verifies that an AI agent is actually connected to the consumer it claims to represent. 
• Could agents eventually skip Experian and get the data somewhere else? He says they can't reproduce it. Decades of longitudinal financial and identity data, plus its provenance and regulatory standing, are what matter when the output drives consequential decisions. "In order to be able to make a decision, you've got to have that trusted data source."

His advice if you're early: 
• Train employees. 
• Set guardrails before deployment. "So much of safety and responsibility comes from the person interacting with the system." 
• Route AI traffic through a controlled gateway where usage can be observed and policies enforced.

Which AI leader should I learn from next?

hits.name: Shruti
hits.hook: 1,200+ pages of the original Chinese Three-Body Problem trilogy, turned into text in a single pass.
hits.original_en:
1,200+ pages of the original Chinese Three-Body Problem trilogy, turned into text in a single pass.

That's what Baidu's newly released Unlimited OCR 2 just accomplished.

Page count isn't the hard part. Any OCR tool can go page by page. The hard part is reading a long document in one pass while keeping track of relevant information from earlier pages, so a table that runs onto the next page or numbering set hundreds of pages back stays consistent. That's where AI document parsers usually degrade.

In Baidu's report, MiniMax-M3 fails past about 223 pages, and Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next lose accuracy as documents get longer. Unlimited OCR 2 stays relatively stable. On MarathonDocBench, built from documents hundreds of pages long, it scored 77.1. The next best model in the comparison scored 33.7.

The trick is Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention (SR-SWA). It works like a person transcribing a book: eyes on the current page, looking back at the most relevant earlier pages. So the cost of each decoding step barely grows with length. At 100 pages it was 7× faster per step than full attention.

The first version already has 10M+ downloads on Hugging Face and 28K stars on GitHub.

What I still want to see: independent runs on messy scans, handwriting and mixed-language PDFs. These numbers come from Baidu's report, and a printed novel is a clean source.

If it holds up, contracts, filings and data rooms could be processed in a single run instead of having to be split into separate documents.

hits.name: Oogie
hits.hook: Turn any photo into a minimalist Japanese manga print poster with GPT Image 2.5.
hits.original_en:
Turn any photo into a minimalist Japanese manga print poster with GPT Image 2.5. 

Prompt: Task: Create a 3:4 Split-Panel Photo-to-Japanese Illustration Poster

Transform the uploaded photograph into a vertically composed 3:4 comparison poster. The upper half displays the original photograph, while the lower half features a Japanese hand-drawn manga illustration with a limited-color print-poster aesthetic, faithfully redrawn from the same photograph.

Divide the canvas into two equal horizontal sections, each occupying exactly 50% of the total height. Both sections must have the same width. The horizontal division should connect seamlessly, with no gap, border, overlap, or decorative separator.

1. Upper Half — Original Photograph

- Preserve the original photograph exactly as it is.
- Do not redraw, recolor, retouch, or add any text to the photograph.
- Scale proportionally without stretching or distorting the image.
- If necessary, crop peripheral background areas first while preserving the main subject and important visual details.
- If the aspect ratio cannot be accommodated without compromising essential content, extend the edges with a light grayish-cream background. Never invent or reconstruct missing parts of the original photograph.

2. Lower Half — Japanese Hand-Drawn Illustration

Redraw the photograph as a Japanese-inspired hand-drawn manga illustration with a minimalist, limited-color screen-print poster aesthetic.

The original photograph is the exclusive source of the subject's identity, appearance, pose, structure, composition, layout, and relationships between objects.

For people:

- Preserve recognizable facial shape, hairstyle silhouette, expression, pose, gestures, and clothing category.
- Simplify the face into clean manga-style shapes.
- Render hair as grouped, flowing masses rather than individual strands.
- Express clothing through elegant, simplified fashion silhouettes.

For animals:

- Preserve the species, body proportions, distinctive coat-color patterns, and pose.
- Use simplified contours and flat color blocks to retain recognizability.

For objects:

- Preserve the original silhouette, essential structural details, and proportions.

For landscapes and scenery:

- Preserve the terrain, architecture, distribution of visible elements, and spatial depth.
- Redraw the main landscape as a cohesive illustration rather than reducing it to an isolated object.

Preserve all visible contact, overlap, and occlusion relationships. Depict only what is visible in the source photograph. Do not introduce new subjects, props, gestures, or structures outside the original image.

If an additional style reference is provided, use it only for drawing technique, color palette, and layout. Never copy its subjects or content.

3. Linework and Color Treatment

Use a consistent combination of delicate ink outlines, naturally simplified shapes, and limited-color flat fills.

- Ink outline: Near-black "#02030B", with varied pressure, subtle line-weight changes, occasional pauses, and slightly irregular hand-drawn edges.
- Keep internal lines minimal, retaining only the structural details necessary to define form.
- Use clean, continuous, opaque color blocks.
- Merge shadows into a small number of hard-edged color shapes.
- Avoid individual hair strands, dense hatching, photorealistic textures, and excessive decorative detail.
- Preserve the subject's essential natural colors and distinctive identifying color patterns.

Lower-panel background: Light grayish cream "#ECEDE5".

Primary accent: Warm red "#E9444B".

Secondary accent: Muted blue-gray "#5296BD".

Use red as the dominant accent and blue sparingly. Ensure that accent colors complement the subject without compromising its recognizability.

Simplify the background to the cream paper tone, retaining only the environmental details needed to communicate the setting, explain the action, and preserve spatial relationships. For landscape photographs, translate the principal scenery into the illustration rather than omitting it.

4. Lower Panel — Minimalist Poster Layout

Create a refined editorial composition with a small illustration surrounded by generous negative space.

- Treat the subject and essential environmental elements as one cohesive illustration.
- Scale the complete illustration proportionally and center it within the lower panel.
- Keep the entire illustration group within approximately 65–70% of the panel width and 60–65% of the panel height.
- Fit the illustration within these limits without stretching or distorting it.
- Maintain generous light grayish-cream margins on all sides.
- Do not let the illustration touch the edges or fill the entire panel.
- Do not use large background color blocks to fill the empty space.
- Do not add a border around the illustration.

The overall layout should resemble a thoughtfully designed Japanese art-print poster: restrained, balanced, airy, and visually sophisticated.

5. Handwritten Typography

Add two small handwritten text elements within the negative space of the lower panel.

Top area: Place a small, delicate, near-black handwritten phrase, such as:

“FROM LIFE TO LINES.”

Beside the illustration: Add an even smaller, casual handwritten phrase, such as:

“another way to see.”

Generate both phrases automatically based on the subject, setting, and emotional atmosphere of the original photograph. The wording should feel concise, natural, poetic, and contextually relevant.

The example phrases are references for tone and placement only. Do not use them automatically if a more fitting caption can be generated.

Typography must remain subtle and secondary to the illustration. Use a natural handwritten style with fine, slightly imperfect strokes. Ensure all generated text is spelled correctly and legible.

6. Final Output Requirements

- Aspect ratio: 3:4 portrait.
- Upper half: 50% of canvas height, displaying the untouched original photograph.
- Lower half: 50% of canvas height, displaying the Japanese-inspired hand-drawn illustration.
- Equal panel widths, seamless horizontal transition, no gap, no frame, and no overlap.
- Consistent minimalist Japanese manga linework and limited-color print-poster styling.
- Small, centered illustration with generous cream-colored negative space.
- Subtle, context-aware handwritten typography in the lower panel.

Core principle: The original photograph determines what is depicted. The illustration style determines how the lower half is redrawn. Preserve the source's identity and composition while transforming the lower panel into an elegant, minimalist Japanese illustration poster.

hits.name: Trace Cohen
hits.hook: Venture capital has entered a pretty funny phase.
hits.original_en:
Venture capital has entered a pretty funny phase.

A startup raises at a $2B valuation with barely any revenue.

Six months later, someone offers shares through an SPV at $3B, plus fees and carry.

Suddenly everyone wants access because the deal is “hard to get.”

But what exactly changed about the business?

Sometimes the technology is genuinely incredible and the opportunity is enormous.

Other times, we’re just watching investors sell scarcity to other investors at increasingly ridiculous prices.

Access to a hot deal isn’t the same thing as getting a good deal.

hits.name: Trace Cohen
hits.hook: Anthropic’s IPO could create some of the biggest VC returns we’ve ever seen, but the really crazy part is how much a SINGLE investment could return relative to an entire fund.
hits.original_en:
Anthropic’s IPO could create some of the biggest VC returns we’ve ever seen, but the really crazy part is how much a SINGLE investment could return relative to an entire fund.

Assuming a $1.5T IPO valuation, here’s how the math looks:

Spark Capital (2023 Series C)
• Initial investment: $75M at ~$5B valuation
• Fund: $1.4B Growth Fund IV (2022 vintage)
• Estimated stake value: ~$10.9B
• Gross return: ~145x
• Equivalent to ~7.8x the entire fund size

Sound Ventures (2023 Series C)
• Initial investment: ~$35M at ~$5B valuation
• Fund: $240M AI Fund (2023 vintage)
• Potential value: ~$4.5B–$7.5B
• Gross return: ~129–214x
• Equivalent to ~19–31x the fund size

Menlo Ventures (2024 Series D)
• Investment: $500M+ at ~$15B valuation
• 2023 fund family: $1.35B
• Estimated total firm stake: ~$21.8B
• Series D alone could generate tens of billions in gross value, although much of the investment was syndicated through SPVs.

Lightspeed (2025 Series E)
• Led $3.5B round at $61.5B valuation
• Entry-to-IPO valuation increase: ~24x
• Exact initial check and fund allocation undisclosed.

ICONIQ (2025 Series F)
• Reported aggregate investment: ~$6B
• Estimated stake value: ~$26.4B
• Blended gross return: ~4.4x

Coatue (2025 Series F)
• Reported aggregate investment: ~$4.75B
• Estimated stake value: ~$11.7B
• Blended gross return: ~2.5x

Sequoia (2026 Series G)
• Reported investment: ~$3B at ~$380B valuation
• Entry-to-IPO valuation increase: ~3.9x

These are illustrative paper values, not realized returns. Some positions span multiple funds and SPVs, and actual ownership dilution matters.

What’s fascinating is that Spark’s early investment could be worth nearly 8x its entire $1.4B fund, while Sound Ventures’ position could theoretically be worth more than 20x its $240M AI fund.

We’ve spent years talking about power laws in venture capital, where one investment returns the fund.

Anthropic could be the rare case where one investment returns the fund 10 or even 20 times over.

And that’s before considering what Amazon, Google, and the founders stand to make.

I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long.

Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's.

But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries:

Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it.

Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing.

Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications.

Spoke to someone leading AI enablement at a massive retailer.

The #1 problem they’re running into: AI transformation is owned by IT and all initiatives must run through their AI Center of Excellence.

This is causing two parallel issues:
1) Employees outside of IT aren’t given the tooling/infra needed to automate anything beyond simple workflows/use cases (read: citizen developer SDLC)
2) Rolling out AI is bottlenecked by ITs ability to own and approve every initiative

This challenge is incredibly common across enterprises & you can quickly appreciate why…

On one hand, you can empathize with IT. They’re not incentivized to take risks & embrace disruption, so the risk-return of decentralizing AI implementation cross-org is not obvious.

On the other hand, an enterprise’s ability to metabolize raw intelligence is metered by its corporate SDLC. IT is often the bottleneck in that SDLC and it’s not hyperbolic to say that poses existential risk for the enterprise.

hits.name: Shruti
hits.hook: Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.
hits.original_en:
Yann LeCun was right & nobody in this industry wants to say it out loud.

109 million parameters beat 72 billion.

He has spent years saying scale is not the thing that makes a model understand the world. Meta bet the other way. He left in November and started his own lab in Paris.

Last Thursday he published the proof.

The theory everyone has been running on since 2024 is that if you train models big enough, on text, on images, on sound, they all end up with the same picture of reality inside them. Size does it. Nobody ever proved that part.

Randall Balestriero and LeCun proved it. And the proof says size was never doing the work.

What does the work is which two things you show a model together.

A photo and the caption of that photo are two views of one thing. Models trained on pairs like that get there fast.

Two paragraphs pulled from the same document are not two views of one thing. Models trained on those get there slowly and expensively.

Next word prediction is the second kind. That is what every chatbot in the world runs on.

In their tests the first method reached the same understanding after 21.6 million examples. Next word prediction needed 900 million.

And a 109 million parameter text model ended up closer to an image model's view of the world than a 72 billion parameter language model was.

660 times smaller.

hits.name: Peter Yang
hits.hook: I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.
hits.original_en:
I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.

Some takes I loved:

1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.”

Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat.

2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?”

Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place.

3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?”

Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first.

4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.”

Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.”

5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.”

Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first.

6. “Let your kid be your creative director.”

Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode. It’s live on Spotify.

"Goal: [what you want, and what it's for]

Context: [who it's for, what good looks like]

> Claude then code it, lower chance to get it wrong

hits.hook: A startup growing 100% a year can actually become less attractive to acquire.
hits.original_en:
A startup growing 100% a year can actually become less attractive to acquire.

Imagine a company doing $20M in revenue, growing 100% annually, with an acquisition offer of $200M.

Pretty incredible outcome.

But management decides to raise another round at a $500M valuation instead.

Two years later, revenue hits $80M, but growth slows to 30%. Buyers now offer 4x revenue, or $320M.

The company quadrupled its revenue, doubled down on its ambitions, and ended up with a potential exit worth less than its last funding valuation.

All hypothetical, but the math is very real.

Sometimes the hardest part of building a billion-dollar company is knowing when you’ve already built a great one.

Stop billing hourly. Package your asset, set the outcome, and anchor between $3k and $7k.

outsiders.hook: SOS 🆘 Grok Bot users had a rough week 💀
outsiders.original_en:
SOS 🆘 Grok Bot users had a rough week 💀

Many of them burned through 100% of their weekly usage days before the reset, including people who say they never hit the limit. One user watched his meter leap from 44% to 87% in just 24 minutes.

When one of them asked Elon for a reset, he didn’t hand one out. Instead, he got refreshingly honest and said the cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue 😱

That one line tells you a lot.

Notice what he didn’t say. He didn’t blame a shortage of chips.

He said the bot costs more to run than it earns. That turns this into a question about money, not hardware: what else could those chips be earning right now?

Grok Bot is a hungry product. It isn’t a chatbot sitting around waiting for your next question.

It’s an agent with its own cloud computer, and it keeps grinding through tasks long after you close the app.

SpaceX says it hit 800,000 paid weekly users in October, more than doubling in a single month. Even more striking, people use it more every week, not less.

Yet it’s sold on flat monthly plans, with the main X Subscription tiers at $30, $100 and $200. That’s an all-you-can-eat buffet price for customers whose appetites keep growing.

Here’s where it gets interesting.

On that same earnings call, SpaceX revealed that new compute pays for itself in under a year at today’s rental prices.

Elon said the goal is to split compute roughly 50-50 between SpaceX’s own products and outside customers. SpaceX has even pushed some of its inference work out to other cloud providers so it can keep more of its own chips for training.

Think about what that means.

Every GPU hour Grok Bot burns is an hour SpaceX could have rented out at market rates, and those rates keep climbing.

According to SemiAnalysis, a one-year H100 rental contract jumped almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026.

That chip came out in 2022. Hardware is supposed to get cheaper as it ages, yet this one got more expensive.

Now run the numbers on a newer Blackwell B200, which rents for around $6 an hour. At that rate, a $30 subscription buys roughly five hours of one B200 per month.

To be fair, a single bot doesn’t tie up a whole GPU, since servers share each chip across many users at once. But an agent working all week chews through those five hours far faster than any chat window ever could.

To me, this is a pricing problem far more than a demand problem.

Only 4.5% of US consumers paid for a personal ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude subscription as of August, but that share doubled in just one year.

The appetite is clearly there. In Elon’s replies, some users are asking for $500 and $1,000 tiers, while others want a cheaper, lighter model for basic tasks.

Both camps want the same thing: pricing tied to how much work the bot actually does.

My bet is that AI agent pricing will start looking a lot less like Netflix and a lot more like your electric bill.

And for SpaceX, that’s a fantastic problem to have. When the fastest-growing product Elon has ever seen can’t cover the cost of running on SpaceX’s own chips, it tells you just how valuable those chips have become.

a $30 plan covers roughly five hours a month of one B200 rented at around $6 an hour

that gap is why Grok Bot users got squeezed this week. weekly meters hit 100% days ahead of reset, even for people who swear they'd never maxed out. one jumped 44% to 87% within 24 minutes

when someone begged Elon for a reset, he said the bot costs far more to serve than it earns. no mention of a chip shortage, so read it as a money problem: each GPU hour spent on Grok Bot is an hour SpaceX could rent to someone else

what drives the squeeze:

- per SpaceX, October closed at 800,000 paid weekly users, over double the month before, with usage per person rising weekly

- tiers sit flat at $30, $100 and $200, an all-you-can-eat deal for growing appetites

- SemiAnalysis tracked a one-year H100 contract climbing almost 40% from October 2025 to March 2026, on a 2022 chip

- fresh compute earns back its cost in under a year at today's rates, and Elon is aiming for a 50-50 compute split between in-house products and outside buyers

outsiders.name: MyShell.AI
outsiders.hook: $3.47 vs $1.38. same prompt, two video models, and most people picked the cheaper clip as the more real one.
outsiders.original_en:
$3.47 vs $1.38. same prompt, two video models, and most people picked the cheaper clip as the more real one.
that one comparison sums up october pretty well. here’s the rest of the month👇

· video got cheap, and long
openai switched off the sora api on sep 24, so october was the first full month without it. wan 3.0 and seedance 2.5 took the top of the leaderboard, both at 30s per clip, and the price gap between them pays for more drafts per idea.
then kling 4.0 landed on oct 15: up to 30s in one pass, 10 keyframes, 15 references. the skill that matters now is directing: where the shot starts, where it turns, what has to stay the same.

· consistency became a model feature
openai shipped chatgpt images 2.5 on oct 5. google shipped nano banana 2.1 the next day at about half the per-image price, with multi-turn character consistency built in, and retired nano banana 2 on oct 29. black forest labs put out flux 3 image plus open-weight klein.
in september we said: write the identity once, only change the shot. this month the models started handling that part on their own.

so what’s left for the people building on top?
taste. knowing what makes a double exposure read as one image, or what separates a designed glitch from a broken file. that’s the part myshell agents package into one tap.

WHAT IT IS

SIGN IN
[] Desktop: Get started, then Sign In with Cursor in the browser
[] iOS: Login with Cursor, finish in the browser, return to the app
[] Official: Cmd-D turns on voice dictation
[] Official: it is easier to use the remote computer from your phone
[] Use the same Cursor account that should own usage
[] First-run tour asks which tools you use; that only shapes teammate suggestions
[] Computer setup runs in the background, then Meet a future teammate opens

CREATE A BOT
- Testers (XFreeze, Oct 27): import your memories from other assistants (preferences, instructions, writing style, personal context) instead of starting from scratch
[] Open Settings, then General, then Import Memory
[] Follow the steps to bring over your context from the other assistant
[] Ask your Bot what it now remembers and correct anything wrong
- Testers (tibor_tee, Oct 7): the Grok Bot Marketplace is a shelf of ready-made bots for engineering, sales, marketing, design, product, recruiting, operations and personal life; pick one for a job you keep putting off
[] New in the sidebar, or Cmd/Ctrl+N
[] In New chat, choose Create new agent
[] Edit Profile: name, title, description, avatar
[] Give a short name, one primary job, and how it should work
[] Description = standing rules (never send without approval)
[] Chat messages = this-task instructions (draft follow-ups for these 12 accounts)
[] Focused Bots beat one catch-all General Helper
[] Testers (XFreeze): do not design a Bot from scratch; ask a Bot to create a capable one for you (it already has your context)
[] Pin important Bots; hide unused ones (hiding does not pause routines)
[] Duplicate a Bot to reuse a role for a new scope (copy does not include memory or history)
[] Delete only if you are sure; files and logins on the shared computer stay
[] Account limit: 50 Bots and group chats combined
[] Name language can steer reply language (bookmark testers reported this)
[] Official Elon / Grok Bot team (Sep 17): Grok Bot now has a voice — talk to bot
[] Official (bot, Sep 18): Grok Bot can now send you voice notes
[] Testers (GrokBotDev): Official Marketplace launched (about 69 bots listed; community has catalogued 420+ searchable from a Bot)
HOW TO WRITE A TASK
- Testers (Michael_Fenech_, Oct 3): run a monthly human-dependency audit. Ask your chief-of-staff Bot to review the last 30 days and find every place work waited on you
[] Look for jobs it could start alone, decisions it keeps waiting on, info it keeps asking for, repeat approvals, hand-offs between Bots and checks that could be routines
[] Label each one Keep me in, Teach, Systemise, Automate or Escalate only
[] Change nothing yet; review the biggest ones first, one at a time
- Testers (AlexFinn, Oct 4): reverse prompting loop. Ask "Based on what you know about me and my work, what are 5 productive things you could do for me?", pick one, and repeat; more connectors (especially email) make it stronger
[] Outcome: what should be finished
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): Grok Bot meters agent steps and tokens, not messages — vague tasks wander and burn the week; scope with Task / Work in / Context / Done means / first N items then stop
[] Sources: which apps, sites, files, or chats matter
[] Constraints: what it must not do, or must ask first
[] Deliverable: what it should return
[] Review point: when it should stop for you
[] Safe first task: attach a file and ask for a cited summary; do not change the file
[] Next task: one real tool, read-only, with a sign-in handoff if needed
[] After a good result, name the lasting format preference in chat
[] Then save it as a skill or routine
[] Official bot examples: email cleanup, Starlink-likely flights, build a site then buy the domain and deploy, meeting notes, sales prospecting, refunds, podcast audio digest
[] Testers: one clear job, explicit allowed sources, no-guessing rule, approval gate before any real action
[] Testers: 5 calibrations - confidence threshold, checkpoint long tasks, show negative examples, gate destructive actions separately, test edge cases first
[] Testers (AlexFinn): anything you are about to do on your computer, ask Grok Bot first

AGENT COMPUTER AND LOGINS
- Testers (testerlabor, Oct 12): wish — two Grok Bot email addresses per user, one personal and one work
[] Open Agent Computer from the conversation to watch the desktop
[] Official Elon (Sep 14): Grok Bot now lets you route through your local machine (Bot Computer egress via your IP / local machine)

[] Official (bot, Sep 8): fill out forms and logins for your Bot without ever leaving the chat, with support for any password manager
[] Testers (XFreeze): when a site needs your account, Bot pauses; you auth with 1Password / Apple Passwords / any manager; Bot continues — no pasting credentials into chat
[] Grok Bot team (poteto, Sep 9): account switching is finally here
[] Official (bot, Sep 9): Share a file directly with Grok Bot on mobile

[] Prefer a connector/plugin when one exists; use the browser when it does not
[] Official (bot, Sep 11): Grok Bot can now search and act across Microsoft Teams for you
[] Keep durable files in /workspace with clear project folders
[] Settings → Beta: Update Agent Computer (preserve state), Recover, or Reset (can lose recent work)
[] The cloud computer is not your Mac or Windows machine

[] Testers (XFreeze): take over that same cloud computer from your phone without being at the laptop

PLUGINS AND CONNECTORS
- Testers (ScottyBeamIO, Oct 16): Grok Bot can read X Chat messages and message requests (sort inbox, review requests, reply)

[] Routine = when to run that work (schedule or event)

[] Create a routine on the Bot that should own the job
[] Confirm owner, schedule, time zone, input, result, approval, and missing-data behavior
[] Event triggers (Slack, GitHub) are separate from plugins and need their own connection
[] Keep event matchers narrow; avoid every new message
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): never trigger on every new message (docs warn broad listeners eat usage); pick one channel and one keyword; audit forgotten dailies
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): add to every routine — if the source is unavailable, report the failure instead of using old data; test run before you schedule
[] Test run does real work; use safe inputs
[] Testers quoting docs: Test can send real emails to real clients; Stop is a brake, not a rewind
[] View conversation details → Routines to pause, edit, inspect, or delete
[] A Bot can own 50 routines; last 20 run records are kept
[] Deleting a routine has no undo
[] Long absence can pause unattended routines until you confirm

MULTI BOT TEAMS

- Testers (hoshinoxbt, Oct 11): SpaceXAI engineer Lauren Tan's 50-minute workshop on running a team of 20+ Bots (Chief of Staff, PM, specialist workers): single agent, then loops, graphs, autonomous team
- Testers (0xCodez, Oct 11): a shared reverse-engineering setup (PDF) for Grok Bot agent teams; tester claim, check the source before using
[] Official / Testers: Team Bots public beta — shared AI teammates for Teams/Enterprise
[] Start with one Bot that owns an end-to-end outcome

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
